title: Growth of higher permanental compounds at fixed rank
shortTitle: How far permanental compounds can exceed the permanent
oneLine: Order (log n)^k for eigenvalues and (log n)^(k−1) for 0/1 tests at every fixed k, exact exponential rates in the bulk, and a flat real rank-three plateau at e²/6
abstract: Split the n indices of a positive semidefinite Gram matrix A into a group of k and the rest. The k-th permanental compound C_k(A) multiplies the permanent of each k-by-k block by the permanent of the complementary block; every row sums to per A, so the permanent is always an eigenvalue. Bapat and Sunder (1986) conjectured for k = 1, and Pate (2008) for every k, that it is the largest, and Pate also stated that 0/1 tests never beat it. Counterexamples are known (Drury, Tran, Chalmers), and an earlier Evidence Press release found the sharp growth for k = 1 and asked, as its Open Problem 3, for the growth when k ≥ 2 at fixed rank. This candidate answers it. For vectors of fixed dimension (at least three real or two complex), at each fixed k the largest eigenvalue of C_k(A) can exceed the permanent by a factor of order (log n)^k and the best 0/1 test by order (log n)^(k−1), and by no more; at complex rank two the eigenvalue factor is (log n)^k exactly at leading order. For slowly growing k the k-th root of the factor is about log(n/k). For k a fixed fraction p of n the factor grows exponentially with an exact base for every dimension: e/2 ≈ 1.359 at p = ½ in general, but flat at e²/6 ≈ 1.2315 for real three-dimensional vectors for every p between ⅓ and ⅔. Real rank three and complex rank two are the smallest ranks with any violation; an exactly checked real example of order 152 breaks Pate's 0/1 statement for k = 2. Limits: fixed-k constants are exact only at complex rank two; results are asymptotic in n; the refutation of Pate's 0/1 statement for k ≥ 2 was first given in the earlier release. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 23-page paper with a context-first introduction, written proofs of all theorems, limits, open problems and an AI-use statement. Nine Python scripts with recorded outputs. Six use only exact rational or integer arithmetic: the 0/1 witnesses of orders 152, 378 and 10 710, the order-27 spectral certificate for k = 2, exact checks of the trace bound and the 0/1-to-trace inequality on small frames, and the Schur-power multiplicities. Three are numerical (numpy 2.3.5, scipy 1.16.3, mpmath 1.3.0, matplotlib 3.10.7): the real rank-three dual measure to about 40 digits, geometric lemmas with a fixed seed, and the bases behind Figure 1. Every script exits with status 1 on failure, also under python -O. These finite calculations test witnesses, constants and identities; they do not certify the asymptotic theorems. A clean replay in optimised mode reproduced every recorded output byte for byte; raising the order-152 threshold makes its certificate fail. Linux CI reruns all nine, comparing the six exact outputs byte for byte and the three floating-point outputs under a declared tolerance (relative 1e-6 or absolute 1e-12).

keyResults: Theorem 1.1(i) (proof): for unit vectors in R^d (d ≥ 3) or C^d (d ≥ 2) and each fixed k ≥ 2, S_{n,k} = sup λ_max(C_k(A))/per A = Θ((log n)^k) and the 0/1 ratio I_{n,k} = Θ((log n)^(k−1)); at complex rank two S_{n,k} ~ (log n)^k and I_{n,2} ~ log n.
Theorem 1.1(ii) (proof): if k → ∞ with k = o(n), S_{n,k}^(1/k) and I_{n,k}^(1/(k−1)) are asymptotic to log(n/k).

Theorem 1.1(iii) (proof): if k/n → p ∈ (0, 1), both ratios grow exponentially with an exact base for every rank; the base at p = ½ is e/2 ≈ 1.359 for complex d ≥ 2 and real d ≥ 4, while at real rank three it is flat at e²/6 ≈ 1.2315 for every p in [⅓, ⅔].

Corollary 1.2 (proof and exact certificate): at complex rank one and real rank at most two no violation occurs; at real rank three and complex rank two both ratios are unbounded for every fixed k ≥ 2; a real rank-three matrix of order 152 has 0/1 ratio above 1.0049 for k = 2. Theorems 9.1 and 10.1 give exact rates for ordered partitions into any fixed number of parts and lower bounds for individual Schur-power blocks.

Credit and limits: the refutation of Pate's 0/1 statement for every k ≥ 2 was first given in the earlier Evidence Press release; new here are the growth rates, the minimal ranks and smaller witnesses. Fixed-k constants are exact only at complex rank two (at real rank three the k = 2 eigenvalue constant lies between ½ and 2; best 0/1 constants are open); all results are asymptotic in n.
